title: Buehler Versatile Inc. v. The King (Feb 2023 TCC) Case
subject: Agricultural tractor manufacturer SR&ED appeal concerning whether prototype engineering and testing qualified for tax credits.
keyPhrase: Buehler Versatile v The King 2023 TCC
summary: Buehler Versatile v. The King (2023 TCC 18) is a Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision affecting Canadian manufacturers claiming investment tax credits under the Income Tax Act. The Court found system uncertainty only for the 535-HP tractor, allowing one-third ($972,066) of Project 5's remaining $2,916,197 claim because costs were not segregated by model.
metaDescription: Explore the February 2023 Tax Court of Canada decision for Buehler Versatile Inc. v. The King regarding Canadian SR&ED tax credits.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background
Procedural Posture and Overview of the Dispute

On February 6, 2023, the Tax Court of Canada handed down its decision in Buhler Versatile Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 18 (Docket: 2012-4373(IT)G, frequently indexed in tax literature as Buehler Versatile Inc. v. The King), presided over by the Honourable Justice Susan Wong. The litigation arose from the Minister of National Revenue’s disallowance of Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) expenditures claimed by the appellant, Buhler Versatile Inc., for its 2005 taxation year. The appellant, a Winnipeg-based agricultural equipment manufacturer specializing in agricultural tractors (and, according to the Court, currently the only agricultural tractor manufacturer in Canada), sought SR&ED tax incentives under the Income Tax Act (Canada) (ITA) for engineering and development work conducted across seven tractor projects—spanning its four-wheel-drive (4WD) articulated tractor line as well as its Genesis tractor line—for which the Minister disallowed qualified expenditures totalling $3,591,220.

By the time of the hearing before the Tax Court of Canada, both parties focused their evidentiary presentations on Project 5, designated as the 4WD Phase D Tier II High Horsepower (HP) Tractor (referred to in court filings as "4WD Phase D Tier II High HP"), which accounted for the bulk of the appellant’s SR&ED claim; no evidence was led to rebut the Minister’s assumptions regarding the remaining six projects. Within Project 5, the appellant aimed to design, integrate, and build pilot configurations for a redesigned line of high-horsepower 4WD tractors across three distinct power ratings: 435 horsepower (HP), 485 HP, and 535 HP. The regulatory catalyst for Project 5 was the coming into force of more stringent Tier II emission standards set by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Historically, the appellant’s high-horsepower tractors relied upon the Cummins N-14 diesel engine. Because the N-14 engine was being phased out as a result of the more stringent Tier II emission requirements, the appellant decided to build its new tractor line around the Tier-II compliant Cummins QSX-15 engine.

Building a tractor around the larger and significantly more powerful Cummins QSX-15 engine—particularly at the unprecedented 535-HP threshold—required the appellant to start essentially from scratch, because its existing 425-HP tractor design had already exceeded its design limits by 25 horsepower. Most notably, the larger engine created multiple cooling challenges—requiring a layered/stacked arrangement of the radiator, a separate charge air cooler, oil coolers, a fuel cooler and other components, careful fin-spacing, a redesigned charge air cooler, and two widenings of the tractor—while raising the engine to accommodate it produced a 5-degree operating angle that greatly reduced the lifespan of the LCD rubber coupler (essentially a very large rubber ring in a metal shell); the replacement spring couplers then failed after less than 100 hours against an expected life of over 5,000 hours, with measured torque spikes of approximately four times rated torque. Despite these formidable engineering hurdles, the Minister disallowed the appellant’s entire 2005 SR&ED claim—including Project 5—following a technical review by Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) Keith Chrystall, who concluded that the appellant’s activities were not SR&ED in nature; the Minister’s position was that the activities were more accurately described as routine testing, quality control, and/or product development, although the disallowed amounts were allowed in full as business expenses.
Governing Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework

Under Canadian federal tax law, a taxpayer claiming SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) under section 127 and pool deductions under section 37 of the ITA must establish that the underlying activities satisfy the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. For industrial and manufacturing claimants, qualification almost invariably turns on paragraph (c) of the definition—experimental development—which encompasses work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto, through a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Furthermore, the statutory definition expressly excludes routine activities from SR&ED eligibility, including quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes, commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, and style changes.

To operationalize subsection 248(1) of the ITA, Justice Wong grounded the Court’s analysis in the canonical five-part legal framework formulated by Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839, which was subsequently adopted by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393 and reaffirmed in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72. Under this governing jurisprudence, the Court evaluates first whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Second, if such an uncertainty existed, the inquiry examines whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the Court assesses whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. Fourth, the analysis determines whether the process resulted in a technological advancement. Fifth, and finally, the Court considers whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the resulting outcomes was kept contemporaneously as the work progressed.

Within the first criterion of Northwest Hydraulic, Canadian jurisprudence recognizes the crucial doctrine of "system uncertainty". System uncertainty arises where individual components or subsystems are well-understood or commercially available off-the-shelf, yet their integration into a unified, complex architecture creates unpredictable interactions, interlocking constraints, and emergent failure modes that cannot be resolved through standard engineering calculations or vendor specifications.
Summary of the Court's Final Holding

Justice Wong allowed the appeal in part, delivering a nuanced victory for the taxpayer that simultaneously exposed critical vulnerabilities in how industrial SR&ED claims are scoped and accounted for. Drawing upon the testimony of the appellant’s long-time engineer Allan Minaker, Cummins senior applications engineer James Pell, and the respondent’s expert witness Scott Lagadyn—alongside other witnesses, including corporate witness Willy Janzen, who joined Buhler Industries Inc. in 2006 as corporate controller and later became its chief financial officer—and the technical engineering record, the Court rejected the CRA’s sweeping characterization of Project 5 as mere "routine engineering" with respect to the highest-powered tractor configuration. Justice Wong held that when all individual constituent components were combined into the 535-HP tractor, their individual uncertainties merged into a bona fide system uncertainty in which the system uncertainty was the entire tractor itself. Because all constituent parts needed to function in unison to achieve the appellant’s objective, and because the resolution of the cooling and torsional coupler challenges was not reasonably predictable—as evidenced by the number of directions the appellant went in its efforts to resolve them, ultimately building a customized torsional coupler—the work on the 535-HP model satisfied all five criteria of Northwest Hydraulic.

However, the Court declined to extend this finding to the lower-powered 435-HP and 485-HP tractor models bundled within the same Project 5 claim. Because the appellant’s evidence focused on the 535-HP tractor and no specific evidence was led regarding the 435-HP and 485-HP models—whose horsepower was less than or relatively close to that of competitors’ models already on the market, making system uncertainty either less clear or absent—and because the claimed Project 5 expenditures did not distinguish amongst the three models (with labour calculated using an average hourly rate of $24.78 for every employee rather than actual wages), the Court applied a pro-rata allocation. Justice Wong allowed the appellant one-third of the remaining claimed Project 5 expenditures—$972,066 (rounded from $972,065.67) out of $2,916,197, being the Project 5 claim of $2,958,174 less the $10,617 in labour and $31,360 in contract expenditures conceded by the appellant at the hearing—as qualified SR&ED expenditures for the 2005 taxation year, and held that the appellant was entitled to costs, with the amount left to the parties to agree upon by March 31, 2023, failing which written submissions were to be filed or costs would be awarded in accordance with Tariff B. The decision has since been cited by the Tax Court of Canada in Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King, 2025 TCC 63, where Justice Spiro dismissed that taxpayer’s appeals and contrasted its trial-and-error testing with the methodical dynamometer testing of the cooling system and the focused, systematic resolution of the cooling and torsional coupler issues described in Buhler Versatile.
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

While Buhler Versatile Inc. v. The King vindicated the taxpayer’s core engineering thesis regarding the 535-HP tractor, the disallowance of two-thirds of the remaining claimed Project 5 expenditures stemmed from specific legal, technical, and documentation deficiencies, while the protracted 18-year timeline between the 2005 taxation year and the 2023 Tax Court ruling also reflected a hearing that commenced in September 2019 and whose in-person continuation was postponed three times due to the COVID-19 pandemic before being completed virtually. Analyzing these failures reveals the exact friction points between industrial product development practices and the stringent evidentiary standards enforced by the CRA and the Tax Court of Canada.
Over-Broad Project Scoping and the Commercial Family Aggregation Error

The single most costly technical and legal error committed by the appellant was defining the SR&ED project boundary around a commercial product line ("4WD Phase D Tier II High HP" encompassing the 435-HP, 485-HP, and 535-HP models) rather than around the specific technological uncertainties encountered at the upper boundary of the performance envelope. In heavy equipment manufacturing, engineering teams routinely manage product updates in "platform phases" where a base chassis is adapted across multiple horsepower tiers. However, under subsection 248(1) of the ITA and the CRA’s Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (archived in 2021 and replaced by the CRA’s Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives), the size and complexity of a commercial project do not establish that the entire project falls within the definition of SR&ED.

During the transition from the Cummins N-14 to the Tier-II Cummins QSX-15 engine, the Court found that the 535-HP model—110 HP above the appellant’s previous model and at least 85 HP above any competing tractor—presented a genuine system uncertainty, but it made no comparable finding for the other two models. While the 535-HP variant’s cooling and torsional coupler challenges created genuine system uncertainty, the appellant led no specific evidence regarding the 435-HP and 485-HP variants, whose horsepower was less than or relatively close to that of competitors’ models already on the market, so that system uncertainty for those models was either less clear or absent. By bundling all three models into Project 5 without leading specific evidence or tracking costs by model, the appellant diluted the acute experimental narrative of the 535-HP tractor with work on the 435-HP and 485-HP units that it never substantiated as SR&ED. When RTA Keith Chrystall reviewed the claim, he noted multiple deficiencies in the records provided—finding that the engineering change orders showed that engineering work was done but did not show how the activities were organized or how they supported a technological advancement, and that some dealt with matters such as licence plates and the colour-coordination of control knobs—and concluded that the activities were not SR&ED, leading the Minister to disallow the entire claim. Even at trial, the lack of specific evidence of system uncertainty for the 435-HP and 485-HP models resulted in the disallowance of two-thirds of the remaining claimed Project 5 expenditure pool of $2,916,197, representing $1,944,131 in disallowed expenses.
Blurring Component Adaptation with System Uncertainty in Technical Narratives

During the audit and at trial, a central question was whether integrating third-party, commercially available components—the Cummins QSX-15 engine and couplers designed with feedback from Torsion Control—into a new tractor could transcend "routine engineering"; the Court held that the appellant’s need to comply with Cummins’ parameters did not make the project a Cummins project, nor did Torsion Control’s feedback make it a Torsion Control project. The CRA consistently maintains that integrating vendor-supplied components using known techniques and standard testing procedures represents routine engineering or commercial product development. The appellant’s documentation suffered from deficiencies identified by RTA Chrystall: the engineering change orders it provided showed that engineering work had been done but did not convey how the various engineering activities were organized or how they supported the achievement of a technological advancement, and the appellant’s tax advisor acknowledged that presenting emails and meeting-minute excerpts as contemporaneous records would likely not be well received by the CRA.

As highlighted in subsequent commentary on the ruling and in CRA policy, a claimant asserting system uncertainty cannot merely point to the complexity of assembling numerous subsystems. Instead, the claimant must prove that when the individual components are combined, their individual uncertainties merge into a holistic system uncertainty where interlocking spatial, thermal, and mechanical constraints prevent predictable resolution. In Buhler Versatile, the taxpayer only overcame the Minister’s characterization of its work as routine testing, quality control, and product development at trial by demonstrating that although the techniques and testing methods themselves were known, the resolution of the system uncertainty was not reasonably predictable, as shown by the number of directions the engineering team went in resolving the cooling and torsional coupler challenges on the 535-HP unit—including moving from the LCD rubber coupler to spring couplers and ultimately to a customized, one-piece spring coupler. Had this distinction between known testing methods and unpredictable system behavior been rigorously framed in the original Form T661 claim submission, the administrative disallowance could have been mitigated prior to litigation.
Conflation of a Systematic Approach to Work with a Systematic Investigation or Search

The third criterion of Northwest Hydraulic—whether the appellant’s procedures accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method—was found satisfied by Justice Wong, who reasoned that, in the context of a system uncertainty, the appellant formulated and tested hypotheses involving individual uncertainties, and noted that routine activity is distinguished from SR&ED not solely by adherence to systematic routines but by adoption of the entire scientific method, including intuitive creativity. The CRA’s administrative guidelines and jurisprudence draw a sharp distinction between a "systematic approach to carrying out work" (such as organized project management, professional engineering diligence, or sequential trial-and-error troubleshooting) and a "systematic investigation or search" mandated by subsection 248(1) of the ITA.

RTA Chrystall noted multiple deficiencies in the records the appellant provided in support of its claim, including engineering change orders that did not show how the engineering activities were organized or how they supported the achievement of a technological advancement. To satisfy the legal standard for a systematic investigation, the claimant must prove a disciplined, iterative cycle that begins with formulating one or more specific technical hypotheses grounded in known scientific or engineering facts designed to reduce or eliminate the identified uncertainty. The claimant must then plan and execute targeted experiments or analyses to test those specific hypotheses, and subsequently develop logical conclusions based on the empirical results or findings that drive the evolution and modification of subsequent hypotheses. In Buhler Versatile, although the contemporaneous records largely consisted of test results, copies of emails, and excerpts from meeting minutes—which the Court described as imperfect and incomplete—the Court found them sufficient for the purposes of the work and held, on the basis of those records and the witness testimony, that the appellant was focused and methodical and always knew why it was testing a particular theory.
Production-Line Pilot Builds and Financial Cost-Tracking Deficiencies

The evidentiary record revealed that building the pilot tractors for the 435-HP, 485-HP, and 535-HP models involved utilizing the appellant’s commercial production line facilities to assemble tractors with near-production characteristics. Under the ITA, expenditures incurred for commercial production or routine pre-production runs are strictly excluded from SR&ED eligibility, whereas expenditures for experimental "pilot plants" or experimental prototypes constructed solely to test hypotheses remain eligible provided they are properly tracked and adjusted for any subsequent commercial disposition.

Because the appellant’s claimed Project 5 expenditures for labour and materials (along with a contract amount paid to Deloitte, later conceded) did not distinguish amongst the 435-HP, 485-HP, and 535-HP models, and because labour was calculated using an average hourly rate of $24.78 for every employee rather than actual wages, the amount claimed was, as the Court found, inherently inaccurate and could not be linked specifically to the 535-HP work. Furthermore, the corporate witness testifying on financial and corporate matters, Willy Janzen, joined Buhler Industries Inc. in 2006—the year after the 2005 taxation year at issue—highlighting the evidentiary challenge of defending historical cost allocations when contemporaneous project accounting fails to segregate eligible experimental prototypes from parallel commercial model builds. Faced with an expenditure pool covering three models where only one model (535 HP) qualified as SR&ED, and with the appellant having declined to provide the CRA financial reviewer with additional breakdowns until the technical review concluded, Justice Wong allowed, as a principled basis, one-third ($972,066) of the $2,916,197 in Project 5 costs remaining after the appellant’s concessions.
Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement examined in Buhler Versatile Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 18) against the taxpayer’s specific operational and evidentiary deficiencies and the corresponding standard of proof established by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: Taxpayer's Failure / Vulnerability in Buhler Versatile
Tax Court of Canada's Standard of Proof & Holding

cells: 1. Technological Uncertainty vs. Routine Engineering (ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Q1)

The taxpayer bundled three tractor models (435 HP, 485 HP, and 535 HP) into Project 5, and its evidence focused solely on the 535-HP tractor. No independent technological uncertainty was proven for the 435-HP and 485-HP models.

System Uncertainty Standard: Complexity alone does not infer uncertainty. However, when known components are combined and their individual uncertainties merge into an unpredictable whole—where known testing methods cannot reasonably predict the resolution of interlocking constraints (such as the 535-HP cooling and torsional coupler challenges)—system uncertainty is established.
2. Formulation of Specific Hypotheses (Northwest Hydraulic Q2)

Contemporaneous project records (largely test results, emails, and meeting-minute excerpts) did not explicitly frame engineering design iterations as formal hypotheses, and the CRA RTA concluded that the work was not SR&ED; however, the Court found that the appellant was focused and methodical and always knew why it was testing a given theory, and held this criterion satisfied for the 535-HP tractor.

Hypothesis Standard: The claimant must demonstrate that it generated a specific technical idea or proposed method consistent with known facts as a starting point for investigation, aimed directly at reducing or eliminating the identified system uncertainty rather than merely achieving a commercial specification.
3. Discipline of the Scientific Method (ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Q3)

The Minister characterized the taxpayer’s engineering work as product development, routine testing, and quality control, and the pilot builds used production-line facilities to test manufacturing readiness; nonetheless, the Court found that the appellant adopted the entire scientific method, formulating and testing hypotheses involving individual uncertainties, and held this criterion satisfied for the 535-HP tractor.

Experimental Process Standard: Even where testing techniques are standard, the claimant must prove a structured cycle of planning and executing experiments or analyses, observing empirical failures, developing logical conclusions, and modifying the hypothesis across successive experimental directions.
4. Technological Advancement (ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Q4)

The taxpayer framed project goals around commercial product milestones (launching a Tier-II compliant high-HP tractor line); the Court nonetheless found a technological advancement for the 535-HP tractor.

Advancement Standard: The Court found this criterion satisfied because the 535-HP tractor significantly exceeded what was available on the market and was, for a time, the most powerful tractor of its kind by a significant margin, as further evidenced by the later sale of the associated intellectual property; this finding was made only for the 535-HP tractor.
5. Contemporaneous Documentation & Cost Segregation (Northwest Hydraulic Q5; ITA ss. 37, 127)

Multiple documentation deficiencies were noted by the CRA RTA. Critically, the claimed expenditures did not distinguish amongst the three models (435, 485, and 535 HP) and labour was computed at a uniform average hourly rate of $24.78, preventing the taxpayer from isolating the exact costs of the eligible 535-HP experimental work.

Evidentiary & Allocation Standard: Claimants must keep evidence generated as the work progresses. The Court found the appellant’s imperfect and incomplete contemporaneous records sufficient to satisfy this criterion but insufficient to clearly ascertain the qualified expenditures; because only the 535-HP model satisfied the Northwest Hydraulic criteria, the Court allowed, as a principled basis, one-third ($972,066) of the $2,916,197 remaining after the appellant’s concessions.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the legal and evidentiary lessons of Buhler Versatile Inc. v. The King into actionable compliance protocols for Canadian taxpayers, the following two industry case studies examine realistic engineering projects vulnerable to the exact pitfalls identified by Justice Wong. Each case study outlines a step-by-step remediation blueprint across project governance, technical documentation, contract terms, and experimentation cost tracking.
Case Study 1: Heavy-Duty Forestry Equipment Manufacturer (Zero-Emission Hybrid Drivetrain and Thermal Management Integration)
Industry Scenario and Inherent Buhler Versatile Pitfalls

Northern Timberworks Corp., a Canadian-controlled private corporation based in Ontario, manufactures heavy-duty tracked feller bunchers for the forestry sector. Due to stringent federal and provincial carbon-reduction and Tier 4 Final emissions targets, Northern Timberworks initiates an internal R&D program titled "Project Titan: Next-Gen Hybrid-Electric Feller Buncher Line." The project encompasses three commercial machine classes built on a shared chassis platform: the 350-HP Class, the 450-HP Class, and the 600-HP Extreme-Duty Class.

To construct the hybrid architecture, Northern Timberworks procures off-the-shelf high-voltage silicon-carbide (SiC) inverters and axial-flux electric motors from a tier-one supplier and couples them to a downsized diesel generator. In the 350-HP and 450-HP classes, integration proceeds smoothly using standard vendor mounting brackets and conventional liquid-cooling loops. However, in the 600-HP Extreme-Duty Class, the combination of continuous high-wattage hydraulic felling head loads, extreme ambient forestry debris, and compact cowling geometry triggers catastrophic system uncertainty. Specifically, harmonic torsional resonance between the diesel generator shaft and the axial-flux motor rotor shatters the elastomeric drivetrain damper within 40 operating hours. Simultaneously, reject heat from the SiC inverter and hydraulic oil cooler creates a thermal recirculation vortex inside the cramped engine bay, causing inverter derating despite both cooling subsystems meeting vendor bench specifications individually.

Mirroring the mistakes in Buhler Versatile, Northern Timberworks bundles all three machine classes (350 HP, 450 HP, and 600 HP) into a single SR&ED project claim totaling $3.6 million and builds three near-production pilot machines on its main assembly floor without sub-project work orders; in addition, it relies on an external drivetrain vendor contract that lacks explicit intellectual property (IP) and technical risk clauses. Under a CRA technical and financial review, the entire $3.6 million claim faces total disallowance as "routine vendor component integration," or at best, a two-thirds judicial haircut ($2.4 million loss) by analogy to the one-third allocation that Justice Wong adopted as a principled basis in Buhler Versatile.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step A: Restructuring Project Governance and Claim Scoping

To prevent the dilution of experimental work by routine product line extensions, management must sever the commercial product family governance from the SR&ED project governance prior to the commencement of work. First, Northern Timberworks must establish a dedicated SR&ED Governance Committee comprising the Vice President of Engineering, the Lead Drivetrain Engineer, and the Corporate Tax Controller to isolate the experimental boundary. Instead of claiming "Project Titan (350/450/600 HP Line)" as a monolithic initiative, management must carve out the routine computer-aided design (CAD) packaging and assembly of the 350-HP and 450-HP units into a non-SR&ED commercial product development cost centre.

Second, the committee must define the SR&ED project exclusively around the 600-HP Extreme-Duty Class under a title that reflects the underlying scientific challenge, such as "Investigation of Coupled Torsional-Harmonic Damping and Multi-Phase Thermal Dissipation Constraints in 600-HP High-Density Hybrid Forestry Architectures." This directly aligns the project boundary with Justice Wong’s holding in Buhler Versatile that system uncertainty existed for the 535-HP tractor—where the individual uncertainties of the constituent parts merged into a system uncertainty encompassing the entire tractor—but was either less clear or absent for the lower-horsepower models. Third, management must institute bi-weekly SR&ED Gate Reviews staffed by senior engineers who are actively employed and present during the taxation year, and ensure that financial personnel with first-hand knowledge maintain the expenditure records, thereby avoiding the difficulty seen in Buhler Versatile, where the financial witness joined the company in 2006, after the 2005 taxation year at issue, and inherited his predecessor’s recordkeeping choices. Each gate review must formally document why standard off-the-shelf engineering design methods failed before authorizing the next experimental iteration.
Step B: Restructuring Technical Documentation to Prove System Uncertainty

To preempt a CRA RTA finding of "routine engineering" or "blind trial-and-error", the engineering team must replace generic build logs with structured System Uncertainty and Hypothesis Dossiers generated contemporaneously as the work progresses. Before modifying any hardware on the 600-HP prototype, engineers must archive a Baseline Engineering Limitation Memo that attaches the vendor’s inverter and generator installation manuals alongside standard finite element analysis (FEA) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) models. This baseline dossier must explicitly demonstrate that while standard textbook formulas predict stable operation, physical integration within the 600-HP envelope creates interlocking thermal and torsional constraints that invalidate those predictive models.

Once the baseline knowledge gap is recorded, every design direction pursued to resolve the cooling vortex and damper failure must be logged within a mandatory narrative framework that satisfies the CRA Guidelines and Northwest Hydraulic Questions 2 and 3. Each experimental record must begin with a formal hypothesis statement that articulates the exact causal relationship being tested—for example, proposing that shifting the torsional natural frequency below 18 Hz via a dual-stiffness silicone-viscous coupler while redirecting hydraulic heat exchanger exhaust through a negative-pressure venturi shroud will eliminate resonance amplification without starving the axial-flux motor of cooling airflow. The dossier must then specify the experimental protocol, detailing how known instrumentation (strain gauges, accelerometers, and thermocouple arrays) and load-bank test parameters are deployed to evaluate an unpredictable system interaction rather than routine quality control. Finally, the engineers must attach the raw telemetry plots showing where the hypothesis succeeded or failed, accompanied by a logical conclusion documenting the exact technological advancement achieved and explaining how empirical failure dictated the subsequent investigative direction.
Step C: Restructuring Contract Terms with Vendors and Subcontractors

Because industrial manufacturers frequently collaborate with engine, inverter, or coupler suppliers, poorly drafted procurement and engineering contracts can disqualify expenditures under subsections 37(1) and 127(9) of the ITA if work is deemed performed by the vendor on its own behalf or if the taxpayer receives contractual reimbursement that triggers assistance reductions. To insulate the claim, Northern Timberworks must incorporate explicit statutory language in all subcontracts with specialized Canadian testing laboratories or custom coupler fabricators stipulating that the subcontractor is performing experimental development and support work "on behalf of" Northern Timberworks Corp. within the meaning of subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) of the ITA.

Simultaneously, procurement agreements for the off-the-shelf SiC inverters and diesel generators must be structured as standard commercial equipment purchases, accompanied by a separate Technical Integration Responsibility Addendum. This addendum must stipulate that Northern Timberworks bears 100 percent of the financial and technical risk for system-level integration above 500 HP, and that standard vendor warranty support does not cover torsional or thermal system-integration modifications. Furthermore, the contracts must vest 100 percent of all foreground IP, empirical test telemetry, custom cooling shroud designs, and torsional damping algorithms directly in Northern Timberworks Corp., ensuring the claimant satisfies the CRA’s beneficial ownership and technological exploitation requirements.
Step D: Restructuring Experimentation and Financial Cost Tracking

To eliminate the model-level cost commingling that cost the taxpayer two-thirds of its remaining Project 5 claim in Buhler Versatile, the finance and Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) teams must implement strict accounting firewalls. The ERP system must be configured with distinct Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) codes that segregate commercial platform builds from experimental development: WBS-4001 for the 350-HP Commercial Build, WBS-4002 for the 450-HP Commercial Build, and WBS-9003-SRED exclusively for the 600-HP Experimental System Integration.

When the 600-HP experimental prototype is assembled on the main commercial production line, management must issue a dedicated Experimental Build Traveler tied to WBS-9003-SRED. Only labour hours spent fabricating, instrumenting, modifying, and disassembling the experimental cooling shrouds and drivetrain couplers on the 600-HP unit—and direct materials consumed or transformed in those specific tests—may be booked to WBS-9003-SRED. Standard chassis welding and cab assembly shared with commercial units must be tracked separately and excluded from the claim, or properly carved out if the pilot unit is later converted to a commercial sale.

cells: Project Scoping
Single umbrella claim covering 350-HP, 450-HP, and 600-HP machine classes.
Claim strictly ring-fenced around the 600-HP class where system uncertainty occurs; 350/450-HP classes excluded as routine engineering.
Technical Evidence
Assembly logs and failure reports showing ad hoc part swaps.
Contemporaneous System Uncertainty Dossiers linking baseline model failures to formal hypotheses, multi-directional test telemetry, and logical conclusions.
Contractual Terms
Generic purchase orders with component vendors; ambiguous risk allocation.
Explicit ITA s. 37(1) "on behalf of" clauses, 100% foreground IP retention, and clear demarcation that integration risk above 500 HP rests solely on the taxpayer.
Cost Accounting
Pooled production-line costs across all three pilot models without WBS separation.
Granular ERP WBS sub-ledgers (WBS-9003-SRED) isolating 600-HP experimental labour and materials consumed from commercial assembly-line operations.

body.text: Case Study 2: Enterprise FinTech and Industrial IoT Software Developer (High-Throughput Distributed Ledger and Legacy ERP System Integration)
Industry Scenario and Inherent Buhler Versatile Pitfalls

Aethelgard Systems Inc., a Canadian software engineering firm based in British Columbia, develops real-time telemetry and automated settlement platforms for Canadian energy grid operators. As highlighted in recent Canadian SR&ED commentary analyzing Buhler Versatile Inc. v. The King alongside software jurisprudence such as Clevor Technologies Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 166, the doctrine of system uncertainty is acutely contested in software development and system integration claims.

Aethelgard launches "Project Nexus," an initiative to integrate three off-the-shelf software subsystems—an open-source Apache Kafka event-streaming broker, a cryptographic zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) verification engine, and a legacy COBOL/DB2 utility billing mainframe—into a unified grid-balancing platform deployed across three client throughput tiers: Tier A (1,000 transactions per second [TPS]), Tier B (5,000 TPS), and Tier C (100,000 TPS with sub-10-millisecond deterministic latency).

In Tiers A and B, Aethelgard’s software developers integrate the three subsystems using standard RESTful APIs, vendor software development kits (SDKs), and routine configuration tuning. However, at the Tier C (100,000 TPS / sub-10ms) level, combining the three known software architectures triggers severe software system uncertainty. Specifically, memory garbage-collection pauses in the event broker interact unpredictably with thread-locking mechanisms in the ZKP cryptographic engine and synchronous input/output (I/O) bottlenecks in the legacy DB2 mainframe adapter, causing cascading deadlock states and non-deterministic latency spikes exceeding 450ms. Furthermore, existing software design patterns and vendor documentation cannot predict how modifying lock-free ring buffers in the middleware will affect cryptographic state consistency across distributed nodes.

Aethelgard claims $2.1 million in SR&ED salary wages across its entire 18-person Agile development team working on "Project Nexus (Tiers A, B, and C)." Its Jira ticket repository mixes routine user interface (UI) bug fixes, Tier A/B API connectors, and Tier C kernel-level memory experiments in a single backlog. Furthermore, one major utility client provides $600,000 in milestone payments under a Master Services Agreement (MSA) to deploy the platform. Without remedial restructuring, the CRA will either disallow the entire claim on the basis that system integration of known software components does not infer technological uncertainty, reduce the claim by two-thirds because Tiers A and B represent routine software development, or reduce the qualified expenditures by the milestone payments as "contract payments" under subsection 127(18) of the ITA.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step A: Restructuring Project Governance and Claim Scoping

Software system integration is defined as the process of linking together different computing systems and software applications physically or functionally to act as a coordinated whole. As the CRA’s now-archived Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy stated, the size and complexity of a project by itself does not justify that the work performed falls within the definition of SR&ED, nor does the development of a large and complex system support the inference that an uncertainty existed.

To satisfy the Tax Court’s standard in Buhler Versatile, the Vice President of Engineering must bifurcate Project Nexus into two separate governance tracks at the outset of development. Track 1, designated as Commercial API and Tier A/B Deployment, must encompass all standard SDK integration, UI development, database schema mapping, and quality assurance for the 1,000 TPS and 5,000 TPS configurations. Track 2, designated as the SR&ED Project investigating "Deterministic Sub-10ms State Synchronization under Interlocking Cryptographic and Legacy I/O Constraints," must be restricted strictly to the Tier C architectural bottleneck. Management should assign a dedicated five-person core systems engineering squad to Track 2, governed by weekly Experimental Hypothesis Sprints that remain structurally separated from commercial Agile Scrum ceremonies.
Step B: Restructuring Technical Documentation to Prove Software System Uncertainty

To overcome the CRA objection that the developers merely used known programming languages and standard load-testing tools, Aethelgard must apply Justice Wong’s principle at paragraph 60 of Buhler Versatile: demonstrating that while the techniques and testing methods were known, the resolution of the system uncertainty was not reasonably predictable, as evidenced by the number of directions the appellant went in its efforts to resolve the challenges.

First, the core architecture squad must configure a dedicated Confluence and Git repository specifically for the SR&ED project and commit an initial Architectural Constraint Specification. This document must prove empirically why standard horizontal scaling, caching, and vendor SDK configurations fail at 100,000 TPS due to interlocking constraints between Java Virtual Machine (JVM) garbage collection, ZKP central processing unit (CPU) saturation, and mainframe lock contention. Second, management must enforce automated Git-linked hypothesis logs so that no code branch under the SR&ED repository can be merged without completing a structured technical narrative mirroring the CRA’s Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives. Each branch record must identify the exact emergent system uncertainty between subsystems and articulate the formal computer science hypothesis being tested—for instance, hypothesizing that implementing a custom off-heap zero-copy memory ring buffer with speculative asynchronous ZKP batching will decouple garbage-collection pauses from mainframe I/O commits without violating atomic state consistency. The record must then link automated Prometheus and Grafana load-test artifacts comparing predicted latency distributions against actual 99.9th-percentile tail latency under simulated 100,000 TPS stress, followed by a logical conclusion tracing the sequence of abandoned code branches ("multiple directions pursued") to prove non-predictability under paragraph 60 of Buhler Versatile.
Step C: Restructuring Contract Terms to Avoid Contract Payment Disqualification

Under subsection 127(18) of the ITA, a "contract payment" (as defined in subsection 127(9) of the ITA) received by a claimant for SR&ED performed for or on behalf of a customer reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures dollar-for-dollar. To prevent the utility client's $600,000 milestone payment from eroding the SR&ED claim, Aethelgard’s legal counsel must unbundle commercial licensing from core R&D. Management must replace the single MSA with a standard Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) Subscription and Commercial Implementation Agreement restricted strictly to the delivery of standard Tier A and Tier B functionality and commercial configuration services, priced explicitly against the non-SR&ED Track 1 cost centre.

Furthermore, the commercial agreement must incorporate an explicit legal covenant confirming that Aethelgard is not contracted to perform R&D on behalf of the utility client, that the client acquires only a non-exclusive right to access the resulting commercial software service, and that all underlying experimental source code, algorithms, and architectural advancements developed in Track 2 remain the sole and exclusive property of Aethelgard, developed entirely at Aethelgard’s own financial risk.
Step D: Restructuring Experimentation Time-Tracking and Cost Allocation

To avoid a Buhler Versatile pro-rata disallowance across the three throughput tiers (Tiers A, B, and C), Aethelgard must implement contemporaneous time-tracking linked directly to experimental hypotheses. Management must eliminate end-of-year percentage estimates of developer time and instead integrate daily time-tracking software directly into the Git and Jira workflow so that engineers log hours exclusively against specific SRED-HYP-XX tickets corresponding to the Tier C experimental branches. Where quality assurance engineers or DevOps specialists assist in building custom load-generation harnesses for the Tier C experiments, their hours must be logged under a dedicated SRED-SUPPORT code tied to the specific experimental test runs, ensuring their work qualifies as "directly in support" under paragraph (d) of subsection 248(1) of the ITA while excluding routine regression testing of the Tier A and Tier B commercial releases.

cells: Project Scoping
Claiming the entire Agile team across Tiers A (1k TPS), B (5k TPS), and C (100k TPS).
Excluding Tiers A and B as routine system integration; scoping SR&ED strictly to Tier C interlocking latency/state constraints.
Technical Evidence
Unstructured Jira bug tickets and final commit messages lacking hypotheses.
Git-enforced Hypothesis-Experiment-Conclusion logs preserving all failed experimental branches to prove unpredictable resolution.
Contractual Terms
Single MSA with milestone payments for custom development, risking a "contract payment" reduction under ITA s. 127(18).
SaaS/licensing contract restricted to commercial Tier A/B deployment; 100% IP and financial risk for Tier C R&D retained by the taxpayer.
Cost Accounting
Annual retroactive salary estimates pooling commercial coding and R&D.
Contemporaneous daily time-tracking mapped to specific SRED-HYP tickets and isolated from commercial QA/deployment.

body.text: Strategic Conclusions for Canadian SR&ED Governance

The Tax Court of Canada’s ruling in Buhler Versatile Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 18)—subsequently cited in Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King, 2025 TCC 63, as an example of methodical, systematic testing in contrast to mere trial and error—cements three foundational principles for Canadian SR&ED practitioners, tax counsel, and engineering executives.

First, the doctrine of system uncertainty remains a potent legal shield for industrial and software claimants integrating known or vendor-supplied components into high-stress architectures. Where interlocking physical, thermal, mechanical, or computational constraints cause individual component uncertainties to merge into a system-wide unpredictability, the work transcends routine engineering even if the diagnostic and testing techniques utilized are standard in the industry.

Second, the ruling serves as a stark warning against commercial project aggregation. When a taxpayer bundles an entire commercial product line (such as the 435-HP, 485-HP, and 535-HP tractor models) into a single SR&ED project claim without proving independent technological uncertainty across each variant or segregating costs at the sub-model level, the claimant exposes itself to severe judicial pro-ration. Even after prevailing on the core legal principle of system uncertainty for its flagship 535-HP model, the appellant in Buhler Versatile lost two-thirds of its remaining claimed Project 5 expenditures because no specific evidence was led for the 435-HP and 485-HP models and the claimed costs did not distinguish amongst the three models.

Finally, claimants utilizing commercial production facilities to construct pilot prototypes must establish rigorous contemporaneous documentation and ERP cost-accounting boundaries. By proactively severing routine platform adaptations from genuine system-uncertainty investigations at the project inception stage, enforcing hypothesis-driven engineering logs that record every failed investigative direction, and binding work-order accounting strictly to experimental prototypes, Canadian taxpayers can satisfy the five criteria of Northwest Hydraulic and insulate their SR&ED claims against both administrative disallowance and judicial reduction.

outcome: Appeal dismissed; court found insufficient evidence of technological uncertainty and systematic scientific investigation.
